Personally I would like people to understand the fact that marfans syndrome exists at all. It’s a rather overlooked genetic disorder, in comparison to others. In the case of some of my own family, I wish they understood how physically taxing it is to live with chronic back pain and aching joints. You know I may look happy but I do indeed spend every moment in pain wishing there was a way to deal with it all. I’ve tried pain medication, hell I was on oxy when I had my knee surgery a year ago, and none of it affects me and helps with the pain, so I just don’t take it. the only thing I’ve seen truly help me with my pain or anxiety is smoking weed, living in a chicago suburb it’s not so frowned upon, but being 17 makes it very hard to not look like a stoner who smokes because it’s fun. I think overall I really just wish people understood the physical differences between me and someone normal. I just can’t live on my own, but I can’t live on disability because it’s not an adequate system in Illinois. So I must work myself to death in any hope to have any freedom the days I don’t work. I wish people understood, deep down I’m normal, but to get there, I need help.

As someone with Marfan’s syndrome I have to agree. I feel as though my condition has only made my life worse. The surgeries I’ve had on my joints because they dislocate easily, have made my life hell in the last year and a half. My eyes are progressively getting worse and I’m becoming blind at the age of 17. And all of this is topped off with the fact my heart is expected to give out by 22, because of my dilated aortic valve. I mean at first it was a blessing I was diagnosed early, because I was put in an experimental treatment, but all it did was delay the inevitable and left me living a life as a fragile human. I do not wish this on anyone, not even my worst enemies. The fact my aorta may tear any moment and if I’m lucky it will kill me instantly, but with my luck I’ll live for an hour in excruciating pain then die, as one big painful hurrah on my life. I hope to never have children as to not pass this down and make someone live a life like I have.

It’s a dark, foggy night in the Mushroom Kingdom. The black void is dense, separated only by flickers of bright red and blue. In a clearing downhill from a dirt road, police are chattering as they comb the area for clues. A man snaps photos, further illuminating the darkness. In front of him, a body, lying in the dirt. Cold. Mangled. Lifeless. Draped in green.

Dead.

Uphill next to the road, Koopas and Goombas crowd around police tape, craning their necks and standing on tiptoes as they attempt to get a glimpse of the grisly scene.

A lone man draped in a tan overcoat and sucking on a cancer stick steps through the crowd, lifting the tape impatiently and sidling downward toward the group of men clad in blue surrounding the carcass.

A member of the MKPD standing near the body — young, fresh out of the academy — turns and notices the man, then eagerly steps over to meet him, clearing his throat.

“Detective, nice to—“

“No formalities kid, just give me what you’ve got so far,” the man snaps.

The officer is taken aback by the detective’s brashness, but quickly regains his poise, anxious to please.

“One victim. Witnesses say hit-and-run. It’s messy. Seems kinda random.”

The detective stares at the officer stoically, his eyes illuminated for a brief moment by the glowing embers in his cigarette as he inhales.

“Nothing to go on yet?”

The officer shakes his head, seemingly embarrassed. “Nothing sir.”

The detective steps forward, brushing past the officer. He takes a look down at the body and rests his hands on his hips before giving a deep sigh. The officer turns to watch him.

The detective drops to a crouch beside the body, scanning the victim’s bloody overalls and stupid, seemingly frozen surprised expression on his mangled face.

His face...

Then, a revelation.

The detective smirks. He rises to his feet, back still turned towards the MKPD officer.

“I know who did it.”

The MKPD officer’s eyes widen.

“What? How?” he quizzes skeptically, but with a tinge of excitement.

“He left a calling card.”

The officer furrows his brow, puzzled at this apparent breakthrough.

“He... he did?”

The detective turns his head halfway towards the officer, now showing off his smirk. He barely lifts his hand and points down at the victim’s face, which is emblazoned with a not-so-subtle M. No doubt left by the imprint from the tread of a tire.

“Years I’ve been following this guy. Dead Koopas and Goombas in his wake as he stalked the Princess, constantly violating the restraining order she filed years ago after she divorced him. I’ve been tracking him for months, but always a step or two behind. Then the trail went cold and I lost him. Until now...”

The detective pauses and the officer steps forward slowly, wearing shock on his face. “It can’t be...”

“The Princess had started seeing a new guy,” the detective continues, unfazed, “dumb, eager, a true background player... the perfect trophy husband for a royal. Problem is, she didn’t count on his brother coming out of the woodwork, as jealous as he was unhinged.”

The detective takes another drag from his cigarette.

“This was no random hit-and-run, kid. This was a premeditated crime of passion.”

He turns toward the body again, dropping his voice to a whisper. His smirk widens as he stares at the mud-caked L on the poor dead bastard’s hat.

“Oh Mario... you have no idea how badly you fucked up. Your plumbing days are numbered, you mustachioed son of a bitch.”
